reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Fitzpatrick's Dermatology
clinicalPearls: A rare chronic cutaneous vasculitis presenting as persistent red-brown to violaceous papules, plaques, and nodules
Lesions are characteristically symmetrical over extensor surfaces and joints, notably the dorsal hands, elbows, knees, and ankles
Early lesions are soft and inflammatory but become firm and fibrotic over time as the disease persists
It is considered a chronic form of leukocytoclastic vasculitis with secondary dermal fibrosis
Strong associations include IgA monoclonal gammopathy, HIV infection, autoimmune and inflammatory disorders, and haematological disease
Histology evolves from a neutrophilic leukocytoclastic vasculitis to a fibrotic picture in older lesions
Dapsone is often strikingly effective, reflecting the neutrophilic nature of the infiltrate
reference.pathophysiology: Erythema elevatum diutinum is regarded as a chronic, localised leukocytoclastic vasculitis, probably driven by immune-complex deposition in dermal vessels. Repeated bouts of neutrophilic small-vessel inflammation, with leukocytoclasis and fibrin deposition, lead over time to reactive dermal fibrosis, giving the persistent firm papules and plaques over joints. Circulating immune complexes, frequently in the setting of IgA gammopathy, HIV, or other chronic immune stimulation, are thought to underlie the recurrent vascular injury, which explains both the extensor-surface distribution and the responsiveness to dapsone.
additionalDifferentials: Cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis of other cause
Bacillary angiomatosis or Kaposi sarcoma (especially in HIV)
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy showing leukocytoclastic vasculitis in early lesions and fibrosis in older ones
Serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation for IgA monoclonal gammopathy
Autoimmune and inflammatory disease screening (including for rheumatoid and connective-tissue disorders)
Full blood count and evaluation for haematological disease
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase level before dapsone therapy
redFlags: Detection of a monoclonal gammopathy or haematological disorder requiring haematology review
Newly identified HIV infection needing specialist management
An underlying systemic autoimmune or inflammatory disease
Progressive nodular disease impairing joint function
reference.prognosis: Erythema elevatum diutinum is typically chronic and persistent over years, often waxing and waning; it frequently responds well to dapsone, but relapse on withdrawal is common and outcome is influenced by any associated systemic condition.
pitfalls: Mistaking it for granuloma annulare or rheumatoid nodules and missing the vasculitic basis
Failing to screen for IgA gammopathy and HIV
Assuming a single acute vasculitis rather than recognising the chronic fibrosing course
Starting dapsone without checking glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase status
management: Dapsone as first-line therapy, which typically produces a good response in this chronic leukocytoclastic vasculitis
Measurement of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase activity before starting dapsone to avoid haemolysis
Identification and treatment of associated conditions, including IgA monoclonal gammopathy, HIV infection with antiretroviral therapy, and autoimmune or haematological disease
Alternative anti-inflammatory agents such as colchicine, niacinamide or systemic and intralesional corticosteroids where dapsone is not tolerated or insufficient
Surgical excision of late fibrotic nodules causing functional impairment over joints
Monitoring for relapse on dapsone withdrawal, which is common, and periodic review for evolving systemic associations
